Beyond Masked Sparsity: SNACK Enables Truly Sparse Neural Networks on GPU

Jafar Badour Affiliation: University of Twente Email: jafar.badour@utwente.nl    Maurice van Keulen Affiliation: University of Twente Email: m.vankeulen@utwente.nl    Elena Mocanu Affiliation: University of Twente Email: e.mocanu@utwente.nl
Abstract

Deep neural networks continue to grow in parameter count, driving up training and inference cost on GPUs. Sparse neural networks and Dynamic Sparse Training (DST) promise to reduce these costs, but most implementations rely on binary masks over dense tensors and recover little of the theoretical compute, memory, or energy savings. We propose SNACK, a truly sparse GPU layer that stores and computes only non-zero connections. SNACK exposes a simple PyTorch API for restructuring connections and backpropagating gradients entirely in the sparse paradigm, and ships SNACK-COO, a custom COO-format SpMM CUDA kernel with a batch-to-Streaming-Multiprocessor mapping tuned for the small-batch, high-sparsity regime typical of large-model training and single-stream inference. At the kernel level, SNACK is up to 7×7\times faster than the masked dense baseline (Dense+Mask) and competitive with cuSPARSE, Sputnik, and FlashSparse at 95% sparsity. At 90% sparsity, a single SNACK layer accelerates training by 8×8\times and 3.7×3.7\times, and inference by 4×4\times and 2×2\times, over Dense+Mask and fully dense layers, respectively, while using 72% less memory than dense and substantially less energy. End-to-end, SNACK reduces GPT-2 peak training memory by up to 40% and graph-style inference latency by 4.8×4.8\times over Dense+Mask at 99% sparsity.

1 Introduction

Training and serving large neural networks is dominated by dense matrix multiplications whose cost scales with model size, raising real concerns about energy, hardware, and carbon emissions [46, 44]. Large language models in particular routinely involve weight matrices of size around 10000×1000010000\times 10000, with both training and inference dominated by these multiplications. Sparse neural networks (SNNs) and Dynamic Sparse Training (DST) [33, 8] aim to cut this cost by keeping most weights at zero throughout training, in principle reducing parameters and FLOPs quadratically. In practice, however, most SNN implementations simulate sparsity by applying a binary mask to a dense tensor [13, 16]: the dense matmul still runs underneath, and almost none of the theoretical compute, memory, or energy savings materialize on the GPU. This leaves a gap between the promise of truly sparse neural networks (where weights live in a sparse format end-to-end [29]) and what is actually deployed. Mature high-performance SpMM(Sparse Matrix Multiplication) kernels such as cuSPARSE [37], Sputnik [14], and FlashSparse [45] cover several SpMM regimes well, but the very small batch sizes (down to batch =1=1) typical of memory-constrained DST training and latency-bound single-stream inference on commodity GPUs remain underserved, so many fall back to a dense matmul times a binary mask, recovering little of the theoretical savings. We argue that this fallback should and can be avoided: with a small-batch, high-sparsity kernel, a truly sparse layer saves real time, memory, and energy over the masked-dense baseline. We further argue that for other regimes, current and future SpMM kernels can be plugged into our layer as backends, while still benefiting from its sparse gradient handling and sparse initialization. In this paper, we close that gap with SNACK (Sparse Network Active CUDA Kernel), which contributes two pieces. First, SNACK-COO: a custom COO-format SpMM CUDA kernel with a batch-to-Streaming-Multiprocessor mapping tuned for the small-batch, high-sparsity regime. Second, the SNACK layer: a truly sparse, backend-agnostic drop-in for nn.Linear with a sparse outer-product gradient and a memory-cheap sparse initializer, into which third-party SpMM kernels (cuSPARSE, Sputnik, FlashSparse) or our own SNACK-COO plug in as interchangeable backends. We demonstrate this second contribution end-to-end on a consumer-class RTX 3070 (6 GB): dropping Sputnik into the SNACK layer (SNACK(Sputnik)) trains GPT-2 to validation perplexity statistically equivalent to Dense+Mask (the two backends cannot be seed-aligned because Sputnik’s path through Algorithm 2 consumes a different RNG (Random Number Generator) stream from the dense Gaussian-then-mask path; §5) while using up to 40%40\% less peak memory at η=0.99\eta=0.99, so the same model trains and serves on a card that would otherwise be excluded by the dense weight-tensor memory bill. On a single layer at 90%90\% sparsity (Section 4), SNACK delivers:

  • •

    vs. Dense+Mask: 4×4\times / 8×8\times faster inference/training, 72%72\% less energy, 73%73\% less memory.

  • •

    vs. Dense: 2×2\times / 3.7×3.7\times faster inference/training, 35%35\% less energy, 72%72\% less memory.

End-to-end (Section 5), SNACK further cuts GPT-2 peak training memory by up to 40%40\% and graph-style inference latency by 4.8×4.8\times over Dense+Mask at 99%99\% sparsity. We anticipate that SNACK will serve as a starting point for further work on truly-sparse layers and per-regime SpMM kernels, both on the consumer-class accelerators where the memory bill is the binding constraint and on the datacenter-class hardware where the kernel-choice frontier is still evolving.

2 Related Works

We organize prior work along three axes that bound our contribution: (i) sparsity-inducing training methods, (ii) GPU SpMM systems, and (iii) end-to-end truly sparse implementations. An extended discussion (covering early pruning, additional sparse-format details, and CPU/IPU truly-sparse work) is provided in Appendix E.

Sparsity-inducing training.

Sparsity in deep networks has been induced via post-hoc pruning [18, 9, 10, 60, 27], pruning-at-init [25, 47], and Dynamic Sparse Training (DST) [4, 33, 7, 8, 35], which adapts connectivity throughout training. With rare exceptions, all of these maintain a dense weight tensor with a binary mask [28, 13, 16], recovering little of the theoretical compute or memory savings; [55] attacks this from the optimizer side by storing optimizer states only for active parameters, which is complementary to the kernel-level fix we pursue. Hardware-friendly transformations such as Sparse-IFT [49] and SPDF [48] preserve dense FLOP counts to remain compatible with GEMM, which is orthogonal to the truly sparse direction we pursue. At LLM scale, [1] pretrains high-sparsity Llama variants for efficient deployment, and orthogonally, [59] reduces optimizer-state memory via low-rank gradient projections; both target the same memory wall as SNACK but along different axes (sparse pretraining recipe and low-rank gradients, respectively, vs. a truly sparse weight tensor). End-to-end, these methods are typically validated on language modeling with GPT-2 [41] on WikiText-103 [31] and similar benchmarks, which we adopt in Section 5. We discuss the broader literature in Appendix E.

GPU SpMM systems.

cuSPARSE [37] and Sputnik [14] optimize SpMM for the moderate-sparsity, large-batch regime that dominates dense neural network training; Sputnik exceeds dense throughput starting at ≈71%\approx 71\% sparsity. FlashSparse [45] maps unstructured SpMM onto NVIDIA Tensor Cores, targeting graph workloads at moderate sparsity, e.g. GAMLP-style models [57] on the Open Graph Benchmark [20]. BLaST [39] pairs a fused Triton block-SpMM kernel with a block-prune-and-grow recipe to sparsify Transformer MLPs up to 95%95\% on multi-GPU LLM pretraining, but requires structured (block) sparsity and keeps the dense weight tensor live during training. MOSparse [51] addresses sparse-sparse multiplication (SpGEMM, a different operation than SpMM), and SparseRL [30] synthesizes SpMV kernels via reinforcement learning. Background on CSR/BSR/COO formats and earlier kernel-engineering work [3, 32, 54] is given in Appendix E.

Truly sparse implementations and positioning.

Truly sparse training (no dense weight tensor at any point) has been demonstrated on CPU using SciPy/Cython data structures [29, 6, 2] and on IPU hardware in PopSparse [26], which relies on block sparsity (b∈{4,8,16}b\in\{4,8,16\}) to align with vectorized IPU instructions. On commodity GPUs, hardware-supported 2:42{:}4 structured sparsity (Ampere/Hopper Tensor Cores) caps usable sparsity at 50%50\% and requires re-pruning, so DST methods such as RigL [8] and SET [33], which produce unstructured masks, instead fall back to dense+mask. As summarized in Table 1, the combination of truly sparse, unstructured, commodity-GPU with no hardware-specific sparsity support is, to our knowledge, unique to SNACK. Throughout the paper, “sparsity” refers to unstructured sparsity unless stated otherwise.

3 Sparse Network Active CUDA Kernel (SNACK)

SNACK is a sparse-by-construction layer block (Figure 1) that drops in for nn.Linear and keeps weights in COO format end-to-end. The four subsections below cover the SpMM kernel (Sections 3.1 and 3.2), the uniform initializer (Algorithm 2), sparse gradient computation (Section 3.4), and the PyTorch wrapping (Section 3.5). Appendix F provides the full technical companion: a parallel-efficiency proof for SNACK-COO, a geometric-distribution analysis of the initializer’s expected cost, the complete chain-rule and mini-batch gradient derivations, the CUDA/autograd implementation plumbing, and a summary of how end-to-end true sparsity is preserved across forward, backward, and topology updates.

3.1 Sparse Matrix Multiplication

We adopt a unified notation: A∈ℝm×kA\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times k} is the sparse weight matrix with sparsity η\eta (fraction of zero entries), B∈ℝk×nB\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times n} is the dense activation/input matrix where nn is the batch dimension, and C=A​B∈ℝm×nC=AB\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} is the output. Skipping zeros reduces the dense 𝒪⁡(m​k​n)\mathcal{O}(mkn) cost to (1−η)​m​k​n(1-\eta)\,mkn, so runtime is proportional to the number of non-zeros n​n​z=(1−η)​m​knnz=(1-\eta)\,mk.

Algorithm 1 expresses this in the Coordinate (COO) format [3], which stores each non-zero Ai,jA_{i,j} as a triple, i.e. as three arrays (𝐀v,𝐀r,𝐀c)(\mathbf{A}_{v},\mathbf{A}_{r},\mathbf{A}_{c}) over the

Output: Matrix C=A×BC=A\times B

2. for each nonzero element (i,j,Az)(i,j,A_{z}) in AA do

a. for each nonzero element (j,l,Bz)(j,l,B_{z}) in BB with matching jj

i. Ci,l←Ci,l+Az⋅BzC_{i,l}\leftarrow C_{i,l}+A_{z}\cdot B_{z}

3.2 SNACK-COO: Batch-to-SM Mapping

The standard COO scheme assigns one row of AA per CUDA thread and treats the batch dimension as an outer loop, yielding O⁡(n​m)O(nm) thread tasks and leaving SMs idle whenever n≪mn\ll m. Our proposed SNACK-COO instead launches a 2D block grid (Nb,n)(N_{b},n) with Nb=⌈n​n​z/T⌉N_{b}=\lceil nnz/T\rceil for a thread-block size TT (typically 256256): block (i,b)(i,b) owns the ii-th chunk of TT non-zeros and computes its contribution to output column bb. Thread τ\tau in block (i,b)(i,b) reads the COO triple at index k=i​T+τk=iT+\tau and atomically accumulates CAr​[k],b+=Av​[k]⋅BAc​[k],bC_{A_{r}[k],\,b}\mathrel{+}=A_{v}[k]\cdot B_{A_{c}[k],\,b}. The task pool becomes Nb×nN_{b}\times n blocks (i.e. n​n​z×nnnz\times n thread-tasks), so SM utilization tracks the non-zero workload rather than the matrix height, which is decisive at small nn. Appendix F formalizes this with the parallel-efficiency inequality ϵpSNACK-COO>ϵpstandard\epsilon_{p}^{\text{SNACK-COO}}>\epsilon_{p}^{\text{standard}} for n≪mn\ll m, and shows why batch-wise blocks reduce atomic contention compared to row-wise distribution.

3.3 Uniform Connection Initializer

Most DST methods initialize the mask by drawing an m×km\times k tensor of random numbers and thresholding, which materializes a dense intermediate and can OOM for large layers. Algorithm 2 avoids this: it samples n​n​z=(1−η)​m​knnz=(1-\eta)mk unique index pairs uniformly at random and never builds a dense matrix. The expected cost is 𝒪⁡(ζ⋅n​n​z)\mathcal{O}(\zeta\cdot nnz), where ζ\zeta is the expected number of trials before drawing a fresh pair.

At step ii, the probability of drawing a fresh pair is pi=1−i/(m​k)p_{i}=1-i/(mk), so by the geometric distribution the expected number of trials at that step is 1/pi=m​k/(m​k−i)1/p_{i}=mk/(mk-i). Summing over the n​n​znnz unique pairs and applying the harmonic approximation ∑i=ab1/i≈ln⁡(b/a)\sum_{i=a}^{b}1/i\approx\ln(b/a) yields ∑i=0n​n​zm​km​k−i≈−m​k​ln⁡η\sum_{i=0}^{nnz}\frac{mk}{mk-i}\approx-mk\ln\eta for η∈(0,1)\eta\in(0,1), i.e. essentially linear in n​n​znnz. Collisions dominate as η→0\eta\to 0 (dense regime) but vanish as η→1\eta\to 1, so the rejection penalty ζ=−lnη/(1−η)\zeta=-\ln\eta/(1-\eta) is bounded and small in the high-sparsity regime DST targets. The full derivation is in Appendix F.

3.4 Sparse Gradient Computation

For a SNACK layer with sparse weight W∈ℝm×nW\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}, input X∈ℝn×bX\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times b}, and pre-activation A=W​XA=WX, the chain rule yields ∂ℒ∂W=(∂ℒ∂A)​X⊤\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial W}=(\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial A})\,X^{\top} and ∂ℒ∂X=W⊤​(∂ℒ∂A)\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial X}=W^{\top}(\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial A}). The input-gradient term is sparse-times-dense and reuses our SpMM directly since W⊤W^{\top} inherits WW’s sparsity. The weight-gradient term is the cost driver: a naive outer product produces a dense m×nm\times n matrix the size of the unpruned WW. SNACK instead computes (∂ℒ∂W)i,j=∑t=1b∇Yi,tXj,t(\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial W})_{i,j}=\sum_{t=1}^{b}\nabla Y_{i,t}\,X_{j,t} only at indices (i,j)∈supp⁡(W)(i,j)\in\mathrm{supp}(W), dropping the cost from 𝒪⁡(m​n​b)\mathcal{O}(mnb) to 𝒪⁡(n​n​z⋅b)\mathcal{O}(nnz\cdot b) while preserving SGD correctness (frozen entries see zero gradient anyway). Activation functions operate element-wise and are agnostic to WW’s sparsity [17]. Appendix F gives the complete derivation: the chain rule for ∂ℒ/∂W\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial W and ∂ℒ/∂X\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial X, the entry-wise expansion that motivates restricting work to supp⁡(W)\mathrm{supp}(W), and the generalization to mini-batches as a sum of bb rank-1 sparse outer products.

The matrix on the right is ∇Y⊗X=(∇Y)X⊤\nabla Y\otimes X=(\nabla Y)\,X^{\top}, the entry-wise expansion of the outer product. Dense backprop fills all m​nmn entries; SNACK computes only those at (i,j)∈supp⁡(W)(i,j)\in\mathrm{supp}(W). For a single non-zero ⟨2,1⟩\langle 2,1\rangle, the boxed cell X2∇Y1X_{2}\nabla Y_{1} is the only entry materialized. Across forward, gradient, and topology updates, we maintain end-to-end true sparsity: no step ever instantiates a dense m×nm\times n tensor.

 
(∇Y)​X⊤=[X1∇Y1…X1∇YnX2∇Y1…X2∇YnXm∇Y1…Xm∇Yn](\nabla Y)\,X^{\top}=\begin{bmatrix}X_{1}\nabla Y_{1}&\dots&X_{1}\nabla Y_{n}\\ \boxed{X_{2}\nabla Y_{1}}&\dots&X_{2}\nabla Y_{n}\\ \vdots&\vdots&\vdots\\ X_{m}\nabla Y_{1}&\dots&X_{m}\nabla Y_{n}\end{bmatrix}

Boxed entry computed iff ⟨2,1⟩∈supp⁡(W)\langle 2,1\rangle\in\mathrm{supp}(W).

 

3.5 Implementation

SNACK is exposed as a PyTorch nn.Module that drops in for nn.Linear (Figure 1): forward and backward are wired through a custom torch.autograd.Function backed by the SNACK-COO CUDA kernel and a sparse outer-product CUDA kernel for ∂ℒ∂W\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial W}. Weights live entirely on the GPU as the COO triple (𝐀v,𝐀r,𝐀c)(\mathbf{A}_{v},\mathbf{A}_{r},\mathbf{A}_{c}) and are never materialized as a dense m×nm\times n tensor at any point: initialization, forward, backward, or topology updates. The SpMM backend is swappable: SNACK-COO is the default for the small-batch DST regime, but any third-party SpMM (Sputnik, FlashSparse, cuSPARSE) can be plugged in for regimes where it is faster, while still inheriting SNACK’s sparse outer-product gradient and uniform initializer. Wrapper, kernel, and autograd plumbing details are in Appendix F; code is available at https://github.com/JafarBadour/Snack-SNN.

4 Evaluation and Results

We evaluate SNACK at three increasingly demanding levels: (i) the SpMM kernel in isolation (Section 4.1), (ii) a single sparse layer in a 100100-iteration MLP-style training cycle (Section 4.2), and (iii) end-to-end on GPT-2 and a graph workload (Section 5). Unless stated otherwise, all micro-benchmarks run on an RTX 3070 (6 GB) at sparsities η∈{0.9,0.95,0.99}\eta\in\{0.9,0.95,0.99\} and small leading dimensions, the regime SNACK-COO targets. We report CUDA time, peak GPU memory, energy, and parameter count; per-input-size sweeps and additional figures are deferred to Appendix D.

4.1 SpMM Kernel: SNACK-COO vs. State-of-the-Art

We benchmark SNACK-COO against eleven SpMM implementations [12, 5, 38, 40] from PyTorch (CSR/COO), CuPy (CSR/COO), JAX (BSR), cuSPARSE (CSR/COO), Sputnik (CSR/COO), and FlashSparse on a 5000×50005000\times 5000 sparse matrix at 95%95\% sparsity, against a (batch×5000)(\text{batch}\times 5000) dense matrix, averaged over 10001000 multiplications. Table 2 reports CUDA time at batch 11 across four matrix sizes: Our SNACK-COO is the fastest sparse method on every leading-dimension size we tested and the only sparse implementation that beats Dense+Mask, achieving a 7×7\times speedup over Dense+Mask and a 3.5×3.5\times speedup over the dense baseline at 5000×50005000\times 5000. Figure 2 reports sparsity sweeps at fixed batch sizes {1,2}\{1,2\} and shows the same advantage across the small-batch regime. Appendix D.2 replicates this sweep on a datacenter-class NVIDIA A100 across six leading-dimension sizes (500500–1000010000) at batch {1,4}\{1,4\}: at batch 11 SNACK-COO retains the per-column lead at every size (7.5×7.5\times over Dense+Mask, 3.7×3.7\times over dense at 5000×50005000{\times}5000), with SpMM_CSR(Cupy) closing to within 13%13\% only at {8500,10000}\{8500,10000\}; at batch 44 SNACK-COO leads at {500,1000}\{500,1000\} and is overtaken from 5000×50005000{\times}5000 upward by the two Sputnik variants (within ±10%{\pm}10\% of each other at every size), the regime crossover predicted by the parallel-efficiency analysis (Appendix F) and motivating the swappable backend of Section 3.5.

4.2 Single-Layer Training Cycle

We replace one 10000×1000010000\times 10000 linear projection with SNACK and run 100100 SGD iterations against Dense+Mask (the simulated-sparsity baseline) and Dense (Only). Figure 3 sweeps sparsity (and, for the two latency / per-batch energy panels, mini-batch size) across seven GPU-level metrics; Table 3 pins the same numbers at batch 44. At η=0.9\eta=0.9, SNACK uses only 30%30\% of Dense’s parameters (10%10\% trainable plus their COO indices) and 28%28\% of its memory; at η=0.99\eta=0.99 it is 17×17\times faster and ≈12×{\approx}12\times more energy-efficient than Dense+Mask. Crucially, SNACK’s parameter, memory, and energy costs scale linearly with 1−η1-\eta, while Dense+Mask remains essentially flat: direct evidence that masking forfeits the savings sparsity should provide.

4.3 Numerical Equivalence and DST Accuracy

SNACK is a drop-in replacement: forward outputs and gradients match Dense+Mask up to relative error ϵ≈10−4\epsilon\!\approx\!10^{-4} (attributable to floating-point reordering), so any SNN trained with Dense+Mask can be swapped to SNACK without changes to the optimizer or the loss. Plugged into the DST pipeline of [22], RigL(SNACK) matches RigL on ResNet-50/ImageNet at η∈{0.8,0.9,0.95,0.99}\eta\in\{0.8,0.9,0.95,0.99\} within 0.2%0.2\% top-1 accuracy (see Appendix C).

4.4 Memory Headroom at Larger Layers

We sweep input size at hidden dimension 1000010000, recording peak memory at η∈{0.9,0.95,0.99}\eta\in\{0.9,0.95,0.99\} and the first input size that triggers CUDA OOM (Out Of Memory) (Figure 4). Dense and Dense+Mask OOM at input ≥15000\geq 15000 (inside the hidden-size range of modern LLMs [50]) because the binary mask still requires a dense WW. SNACK avoids OOM at every sparsity tested by storing only non-zeros, fitting the same workload in roughly an order of magnitude less memory at η=0.99\eta=0.99. Granular per-input-size profiles (25002500 –1250012500) and a numerical breakdown at 12500×1000012500\times 10000 are in Appendix D.

5 End-to-end Experiments

We test SNACK end-to-end on (i) GPT-2 [41] dynamic sparse training and inference on WikiText-103 [31] via HuggingFace transformers [53], and (ii) batch-11 GAMLP-style [57] inference on ogbn-products [20]. Backends: dense (cuBLAS), Dense+Mask, SNACK(Sputnik); GAMLP also tests SNACK-COO. Sparsities are layer-local (only c_fc/c_proj per GPT-2 block and the 5000×50005000{\times}5000 GAMLP feature head are replaced; attention, embeddings, norms, LM (Language Model) head, and graph propagation stay dense), so for GPT-2 (small) η=0.9\eta{=}0.9 removes only ≈41%{\approx}41\% of total parameters — an architectural ceiling, not a kernel limit. All GPT-2 runs use a consumer-class RTX 3070 (6 GB) to demonstrate viability on commodity hardware where the weight-tensor memory bill is the binding constraint, so we lead on memory (and, for inference, latency). The two backends cannot be seed-aligned — SNACK(Sputnik) draws only (1−η)​m​k(1{-}\eta)mk non-zeros via Algorithm 2, Dense+Mask draws Gaussian-then-mask, distinct RNG streams with no alignment hook — so we report distributional equivalence over independent seeds, not bit-identity.

GPT-2 training (Table 4): an explicit time/energy vs. memory trade.

SNACK(Sputnik) matches (and slightly better) Dense+Mask perplexity at every η\eta (Δ​ppl∈[−1.62,+0.39]\Delta\mathrm{ppl}\!\in\![-1.62,+0.39] (ppl here is perplexity), due to unseedable initializer divergence) and always cuts peak memory (13661366 vs. 22612261 MB at η=0.99\eta{=}0.99, ≈40%{\approx}40\% monotone in η\eta); the cost is per-step latency and energy, higher at low η\eta (582582 ms / 345345k mJ) and at parity by high η\eta (7171 ms / 88k mJ between η=0.25\eta{=}0.25 and 0.990.99) as the fixed launch / format-conversion overhead amortizes against (1−η)​m​n​b(1{-}\eta)mnb arithmetic — the trade flips toward SNACK exactly where DST operates (per-step energy ratio ≈50×→≈1.17×{\approx}50\times{\!\rightarrow\!}{\approx}1.17\times across the sweep). The point of the trade is not faster steps, it is feasibility: the same recipe places a 124124 M-parameter GPT-2 onto cards that cannot host Dense+Mask at all — on the RTX 3070 (6 GB) used here SNACK(Sputnik) at η=0.99\eta{=}0.99 frees ≈900{\approx}900 MB beyond Dense+Mask’s ≈3.7{\approx}3.7 GB headroom, and the same recipe in principle drops onto a 22 GB-class accelerator on which Dense+Mask OOMs immediately.

GPT-2 inference (Table 5):

SNACK(Sputnik) drops peak memory monotonically from 16101610 to 579579 MB (2.2×2.2\times over Dense+Mask’s flat ≈1255{\approx}1255 MB), keeps latency within ≈1.3×{\approx}1.3\times of dense at η≥0.75\eta\geq 0.75, and crosses into a per-token energy win at η≥0.85\eta\geq 0.85 (−22%{-22}\% at η=0.99\eta{=}0.99): the time/energy/memory trade-off no longer trades — SNACK is at parity (latency) or ahead (memory; energy at high η\eta) on every axis. Deployment consequence: the same model fits in 579579 MB at η=0.99\eta{=}0.99 — under half of Dense+Mask’s 12551255 MB — freeing room for two co-resident copies, doubled context, or sub-11 GB accelerators where Dense+Mask cannot fit.

GAMLP graph inference (Table 6).

Training runs at batch 40964096 via SNACK(Sputnik); the trained sparse weights are then served at batch 11 through SNACK-COO (benchmarks are in Appendix G). SNACK-COO cuts peak memory 2.8×2.8\times and latency 4.8×4.8\times over Dense+Mask at η=0.99\eta{=}0.99 (110.6110.6 vs. 309.9309.9 MB; 0.210.21 vs. 1.011.01 ms), and is 3.63.6–4.3×4.3\times faster and 2.82.8–3.3×3.3\times smaller than the dense reference at every η\eta tested — confirming the per-regime story: SNACK-COO wins at small leading dimension and high η\eta, SNACK(Sputnik) covers larger-batch training.

6 Conclusion, Limitations, and Future Work

We presented SNACK, a backend-agnostic, truly sparse PyTorch layer for commodity GPUs, and SNACK-COO, a COO-format SpMM kernel whose batch-to-Streaming-Multiprocessor mapping targets the small-batch, high-sparsity regime current libraries underserve. The layer preserves true sparsity through forward, the sparse outer-product backward DST topology updates via the memory-cheap uniform initializer, and admits cuSPARSE / Sputnik / FlashSparse as drop-in backends. Layer-wise, this yields up to 7×7\times kernel-level speedup over Dense+Mask, up to 40%40\% peak-memory reduction in GPT-2 dynamic sparse training, and 4.8×4.8\times lower graph-inference latency at 99%99\% sparsity, all measured on a single consumer-class RTX 3070 (6 GB) chosen specifically to demonstrate viability on commodity hardware, at validation-perplexity / accuracy parity with Dense+Mask on the workloads we test. By decoupling the sparse-PyTorch surface from any single SpMM, SNACK turns each new kernel into a transparent layer-level speedup, redirecting research effort toward the kernels themselves.

Limitations.

SNACK-COO is tuned for n≪mn\!\ll\!m and η⩾0.9\eta\!\geqslant\!0.9 in fp32; outside this regime, kernels for larger batches or moderate sparsity (Sputnik, FlashSparse, BLaST) are faster, and the layer relies on backend swapping rather than a single dominant kernel. End-to-end gains are bounded architecturally: only sparsified projections recover compute (e.g. ≈41%{\approx}41\% of GPT-2-small at η=0.9\eta=0.9). Although SNACK, as a framework, due to its flexibility and modularity, can easily integrate Sputnik, FlashSparse, or CuSparse, its advantage on large models is investigated just for one architecture, leaving the other models largely under-explored. Yet, the potential of using it in conjunction with a large batch size is a promising research direction.

Future Work.

Immediate extensions: Tensor-Core SNACK-COO for fp16/bf16, multi-GPU SNACK with sparsity-aware collectives, and a runtime backend dispatcher. The substrate also generalises to sparse attention, MoE routers, quantization-×\times-sparsity, and a Triton/torch.compile port for AMD/Intel.

Appendix

Appendix A DST Background

Sparse training of deep neural networks, also known as dynamic sparse training (DST), encompasses methods that maintain sparsity throughout training by starting from a sparse initialization and iteratively updating the network’s connectivity. During training, a fraction of weights is periodically removed and regrown, allowing the sparse structure to adapt to the learning dynamics. Recent work [13, 19, 34, 16, 11] provides a comprehensive overview of DST algorithms, theoretical foundations, and practical trade-offs, demonstrating their potential to scale deep learning efficiently without significant loss in performance.

Appendix B Sparse Matrices & Sparse Operations

Sparse Matrices are the cornerstone of many DST and Pruning methods. Sparse Matrices are data structures containing compact data representations of a dense matrix with missing elements (generally represented by zeroes).

Sparse matrix multiplication (SpMM) is a popular operation in many engineering applications. It is especially crucial when having large data structures. Experiments added early on by [15] in MATLAB explored having sparse vectors in each row. Assuming we have the following matrix:

A=[003400050]A=\begin{bmatrix}0&0&3\\ 4&0&0\\ 0&5&0\\ \end{bmatrix}

Sparse matrix storage data structure is essential in optimizing memory and computational resources. There are many structures for SpM representation. A prevalent structure is the Compressed Sparse Row (CSR) format. It is used for optimized row-wise storage, reducing memory overhead since memory is optimized to be accessed in contiguous segments [42]. A similar format is Compressed Sparse Column (CSC), which is optimized for column-wise storage. The Coordinate List format (COO) is a simple representation of the storage data structure of (SpM), where non-zero values and their coordinates are explicitly stored [3]. Examples on how each representation is shown in Table 7.

Another format is the Block Sparse Row (BSR). It extends CSR by grouping non-zero elements into blocks. Blocks are usually n×nn\times n in size, and if a block does not contain a non-zero element, it gets ignored. It is less efficient, memory-wise, than other formats but more computationally fast as it improves cache efficiency and parallelism [21].

There are many theoretical architectures for sparse accelerators, such as SpArch, which features a fixed outer product dataflow. Flexagon advances this by supporting multiple dataflows (inner product, outer product) within a reconfigurable architecture [58, 36]. Gamma [56] leverages Gustavson’s algorithm with specialized fiber cache and merger hardware to accelerate sparse matrix multiplication. Recent work by [43] demonstrates custom CUDA kernels for uniform sparse matrix multiplication in extreme classification scenarios, where each output neuron receives exactly the same number of inputs, achieving memory-efficient training with 500K labels on commodity GPUs.

Appendix C Experiment within Condensed Sparsity Training Phase

The flexibility of the SNACK layer allows for fast integration into any dynamic sparse training pipeline. In this section, we provide results integrating the SNACK layer into a CNN-based architecture. Recently, [23] showed that DST can be effectively applied to computer vision tasks under a structured sparsity setup, achieving increased accuracy compared to its dense counterpart. The main motivation behind choosing to integrate SNACK with this work is to show how SNACK is integrable with any DST-based work and it is worthwhile to use it for energy cost reduction and restricted memory spaces environments.

Starting from their reported results, we introduce RigL(SNACK) to train a ResNet-50 on ImageNet. In order to do so, we replaced the last linear layer of ResNet-50 used in the dynamic sparse training regime via RigL with our proposed SNACK layer for the forward pass and backpropagation. The layer replacement was directly performed in the code provided by [23]. We ran all the experiments five times and report the mean and standard deviation in Table 8.

It is worth highlighting that the sparse matrix multiplication using SNACK produces identical gradients to sparse-via-mask, which are used in the training phase alongside RigL. This should be reflected in exact results in terms of accuracy between both implementations. However, as can be seen in Table 8, there are slight differences, due to float operations being handled differently.

Furthermore, we investigate their energy consumption (see Table 9). We observed an improvement in energy consumption of RigL(SNACK) versus RigL(via mask) for sparsities above 90%90\% (i.e 90%90\%, 95%95\%, and 99%99\%). Of course, the small reduction in energy consumption is well calibrated with the expected impact of sparsifying only the last layer computation over the total training requirements in ResNet-50.

Appendix D Performance benchmarks using various SpM sizes

D.1 Effects of different hidden layer sizes

In Figures 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, we show more granular memory, speed, and energy results similar to Figure 3 in the main text. We see the findings that SNACK is faster, more memory optimized, and more energy efficient hold across various input sizes.

Our experiments showcase the efficiency of SNACK across various input size dimensions and a large hidden layer size (10000). Figures 5–9 report on the comparison between SNACK, Dense+Mask, and Dense Only layers on energy consumption, speed, and memory utilization. SNACK achieves drastic improvements scaling with sparsity levels. For example in Table 10, at extreme sparsity level (OPENσ=0.99​ and input_size = 12500)\sigma=0.99\text{ and input\_size = 12500}) SNACK achieves execution times as low as 45.345.3 μ\mus (batch size 1), representing a 13.6×\times speedup over Dense (Only) (618.1618.1 μ\mus) and a 30.0×\times speedup over Dense+Mask (1358.31358.3 μ\mus). Energy consumption also decreases when we use SNACK, from 4.364.36 mWh at 90% sparsity (Dense+Mask) to 0.420.42 mWh at 99% sparsity using SNACK, representing 73% less energy than Dense (Only) and 90% less energy than Dense+Mask at the same sparsity level. Memory usage scales favorably, with SNACK using only 839839 MB at 99% sparsity for 12500×1000012500\times 10000 dimensions, representing 89% memory reduction compared to Dense+Mask (74297429 MB).

D.2 Datacenter-class GPU sweep (NVIDIA A100)

To test whether the SNACK-COO advantage observed on the consumer-class RTX 3070 (Table 2) carries over to a datacenter-class accelerator, we re-ran the same SpMM micro-benchmark on an NVIDIA A100 across six leading-dimension sizes (500500 through 1000010000, square matrices, 95%95\% sparsity, batch 11, mean over 1,0001{,}000 multiplications). Table 11 reports the resulting CUDA times. SNACK-COO remains the fastest sparse method at every size, with the constant-time SpMM_CSR(Cupy) path closing to within 88–13%13\% at {8500,10000}\{8500,10000\}. At and above 5000×50005000{\times}5000 SNACK-COO also beats the dense baseline outright, mirroring the RTX 3070 result. We exclude SpMM_BSR(Jax) because the JAX/CUDA toolchain on the A100 host could not be brought up against the same library versions used in Table 2; all other rows are matched to that table.

Cross-GPU consistency at batch 11.

The A100 numbers in Table 11 preserve the qualitative ordering established on the RTX 3070 in Table 2: SNACK-COO is the only sparse method that beats Dense+Mask across every size, the cuSPARSE / PyTorch / FlashSparse rows trail by an order of magnitude at small leading dimension, and the constant-time SpMM_CSR(Cupy) path remains a strong outlier at the largest size only. At 5000×50005000{\times}5000 SNACK-COO is 7.5×7.5\times faster than Dense+Mask on the A100 (vs. 7.0×7.0\times on the RTX 3070) and 3.7×3.7\times faster than the dense baseline (vs. 3.5×3.5\times on the RTX 3070), confirming that the batch-to-SM mapping (Section 3.2) is not specific to consumer-class hardware.

Batch 44: the regime crossover predicted by Section 3.2.

Table 12 repeats the A100 sweep at batch 44 over the same method set as Table 11 (only SpMM_BSR(Jax) is omitted, for the JAX/CUDA toolchain reason given above). SNACK-COO retains its lead at the two smallest sizes (500500 and 10001000, where n=4≪mn=4\ll m still holds strongly) but is overtaken from 5000×50005000{\times}5000 upward by Sputnik, with SpMM_COO(Sputnik) winning at {5000,8500}\{5000,8500\} and SpMM_CSR(Sputnik DL-opt) winning at {7500,10000}\{7500,10000\}; the two Sputnik variants finish within ±10%{\pm}10\% of each other at every size (mirroring their behaviour on the RTX 3070 in Table 2), and the per-column-best at 10000×1000010000{\times}10000 is 21.4421.44 ms versus SNACK-COO’s 65.5465.54 ms. This is exactly the crossover predicted by the parallel-efficiency analysis in Appendix F: the SNACK-COO advantage is ϵpSNACK-COO>ϵpstandard\epsilon_{p}^{\text{SNACK-COO}}>\epsilon_{p}^{\text{standard}} for n≪mn\ll m, and as the batch grows or the matrix shrinks Sputnik’s structured-sparse SpMM, which is tuned for moderate-batch / moderate-sparsity, becomes the better choice. This is the operational reason the SNACK layer keeps the SpMM backend swappable (Section 3.5) and why Appendix G trains GAMLP through Sputnik but serves it through SNACK-COO. Note that even at this less-favorable batch size, SNACK-COO still beats Dense+Mask on every size and beats the dense baseline at sizes ≥5000\geq 5000, so the kernel remains a valid choice whenever Sputnik is unavailable.

Appendix E Extended Related Works

This appendix expands the discussion in Section 2 with material that we omit from the main text for brevity.

Early pruning, lottery tickets, and pruning-at-init.

Early sparsity work focused on post-training pruning, notably Optimal Brain Damage (OBD) [24] and Optimal Brain Surgeon [18], which removed weights with minimal impact on performance. The Lottery Ticket Hypothesis [9] showed that dense models contain sparse sub-networks capable of learning independently when trained from their original initialization. A complementary line removes weights before training: SNIP [25] prunes by single-shot connection sensitivity, and SynFlow [47] iteratively conserves synaptic flow without using any data; both establish a sparse mask once and then train dense-on-mask, in contrast to the prune-and-regrow loop of DST. Modern pruning techniques [10, 60, 27] compress models for resource-constrained deployment and typically apply binary masks over dense weights to simulate sparsity [60]. SparseGPT [10] enables one-shot unstructured pruning of large language models with minimal performance degradation, without retraining. Hardware-friendly transformations such as SPDF [48] combine unstructured sparse pre-training with dense fine-tuning, achieving a 2.5×2.5\times FLOP reduction. Sparse-IFT [49] proposes drop-in transformations that preserve dense FLOP counts while improving accuracy, but require specialized hardware kernels. The structured/unstructured distinction [52] is central: structured patterns are regular and hardware-friendly; unstructured sparsity is more flexible but harder to accelerate.

Dynamic sparse training history.

Beyond SET [33] and RigL [8], two earlier works are central to the DST lineage that SNACK plugs into. Deep rewiring [4] formalised topology evolution as a sampling process governed by a posterior over connectivities and showed that very sparse networks could be trained from scratch on small benchmarks. Sparse-from-Scratch [7] introduced momentum-based regrowth and demonstrated, on the available hardware of the time, that DST can match dense baselines without any dense pretraining stage. SNACK is agnostic to the specific prune-and-regrow rule: any of SET, RigL, deep rewiring, or sparse-from-scratch can drive its uniform connection initializer.

Memory-efficient LLM training.

Two lines of work attack the LLM training memory wall along axes orthogonal to a truly sparse weight tensor. [55] (MEST) keeps the weight tensor dense at compute time but stores optimizer states only for active parameters, plus a soft memory-economic schedule on the regrowth set; the storage savings stack with SNACK’s, since SNACK additionally removes the dense weight and gradient tensors themselves. [59] (GaLore) projects gradients onto a low-rank subspace before applying Adam, reducing optimizer-state memory at the cost of a periodic SVD; this is orthogonal to SNACK because the savings come from the gradient/optimizer side rather than the weight side, and the two could be combined (a sparse weight tensor with low-rank optimizer states) without architectural conflict. At LLM-pretraining scale, [1] pretrains high-sparsity Llama variants and pairs them with a tuned sparse-deployment stack; their kernel choice (CSR with structured 2:4 fallbacks) targets the moderate-batch deployment regime where Sputnik dominates, whereas SNACK-COO targets the small-batch regime they leave for further work.

Sparse formats and earlier GPU SpMM kernels.

The CSR format dominates GPU-based SpMM implementations and leverages warp-level threads to distribute row-wise computation [3]. Block Sparse Row (BSR) extends CSR by grouping non-zeros into n×nn\times n blocks: it behaves similarly to CSR for small block sizes and trades memory for cache efficiency at larger block sizes [32]. Customized kernel fusion and load-balancing techniques further improved SpMM on GPUs [54]. Energy efficiency in SpMM/SpMV is closely tied to reducing computational load: the less time required per multiplication, the less energy is required to power the GPU/TPU/CPU.

Block-sparse Transformer pretraining (BLaST).

BLaST [39] couples a fused Triton block-SpMM kernel (BCSC layout, Tensor-Core MMA-aligned blk​_​M×blk​_​N\mathrm{blk\_M}\!\times\!\mathrm{blk\_N} tiles) with a block prune-and-grow training loop and a second-order oLLM pruner inspired by Optimal Brain Surgeon [18]. It reaches up to 95%95\% MLP sparsity at a median ≤2.25%\leq 2.25\% accuracy drop and reports a 2.2×2.2\times end-to-end inference speedup for Llama-3.2 across 1616 GH200 GPUs, with up to 4.45×4.45\times inference-memory reduction. BLaST is therefore complementary to SNACK on two axes. First, it requires structured (block) sparsity: the kernel’s speedup hinges on the BCSC block size matching MMA fragment shapes, whereas SNACK targets the unstructured patterns produced by SET/RigL-style DST. Second, BLaST is not truly sparse end-to-end: during training the dense weight and gradient tensors are kept intact and only the pruned forward/backward path runs through BCSC, so the dense-tensor materialization that SNACK explicitly avoids is still paid at training time (and amortized only as sis_{i} grows). The two systems thus occupy adjacent regimes – BLaST for block-sparse, multi-GPU LLM pretraining at moderate batch sizes, SNACK for unstructured, small-batch, high-sparsity training and inference on commodity GPUs.

Truly sparse implementations on CPU and IPU.

Using sparse data structures in SciPy and Cython, [29] implemented and trained with DST a truly sparse Multi-Layer Perceptron (SET-MLP) with one million neurons on a single CPU core, with single-core execution being the practical limitation of their approach. [6] parallelized this approach across multiple CPU cores but reported a hard dependence on CPU. [2] adjusted the approach to autoencoders and showed that a truly sparse implementation on one CPU core can outperform the dense GPU baseline in run-time and energy efficiency, owing to DST’s quadratic parameter reduction. PopSparse [26] leverages IPU hardware to deliver 90%90\%-sparsity speedups. SNACK is, in contrast, the first such truly sparse PyTorch building block on standard GPUs, with no hardware-specific sparsity support required.

Sparse accelerators and adjacent kernels.

Several theoretical sparse accelerators have been proposed, including SpArch’s fixed outer-product dataflow and Flexagon’s reconfigurable multi-dataflow architecture [58, 36]. Gamma [56] leverages Gustavson’s algorithm with specialized fiber cache and merger hardware to accelerate sparse matrix multiplication. [43] demonstrate custom CUDA kernels for uniform sparse matrix multiplication in extreme classification, where each output neuron receives the same number of inputs, enabling memory-efficient training with 500K labels on commodity GPUs. These directions are complementary to SNACK, which targets unstructured sparsity on commodity hardware without architectural changes.

Appendix F SNACK Algorithmic Details

This appendix is the technical companion to Section 3: a parallel-efficiency proof for SNACK-COO (referenced from Section 3.2); the geometric-distribution analysis of the uniform initializer’s expected cost (referenced from Algorithm 2); the full chain-rule derivation of SNACK’s sparse forward and backward, including the mini-batch generalization (referenced from Section 3.4); the CUDA/autograd implementation plumbing (referenced from Section 3.5); and a closing summary of how end-to-end true sparsity is preserved across the entire pipeline.

Parallel-efficiency analysis for SNACK-COO (Section 3.2).

The standard COO scheme creates mm parallel row tasks with the batch dimension as an outer loop. When the layer is much wider than the batch, m>|SMs|⋅warpsSMm>|\mathrm{SMs}|\cdot\mathrm{warps}_{\mathrm{SM}}, many SMs sit idle. SNACK-COO replaces this with a 2D block grid 𝒢={(Nb,n)}\mathcal{G}=\{(N_{b},n)\} where Nb=⌈n​n​z/T⌉N_{b}=\lceil nnz/T\rceil, so the task pool is Nb⋅nN_{b}\cdot n blocks (i.e., n​n​z⋅nnnz\cdot n thread tasks). The work distribution per SM becomes

Nb⋅n|SMs|=⌈n​n​z/T⌉⋅n|SMs|,\frac{N_{b}\cdot n}{|\mathrm{SMs}|}=\frac{\lceil nnz/T\rceil\cdot n}{|\mathrm{SMs}|},

which scales with the non-zero workload rather than with the matrix height mm. Within a block, thread τ\tau in block (i,b)(i,b) reads the COO triple at index k=i​T+τk=iT+\tau (k<n​n​zk<nnz) and atomically updates CAr​[k],b+=Av​[k]⋅BAc​[k],bC_{A_{r}[k],b}\mathrel{+}=A_{v}[k]\cdot B_{A_{c}[k],b}. The time complexity remains 𝒪⁡(n​n​z⋅n)\mathcal{O}(nnz\cdot n), but the parallel efficiency

ϵp=Tseq|SMs|⋅Tpar,ϵpSNACK-COO>ϵpstandard\epsilon_{p}=\frac{T_{\mathrm{seq}}}{|\mathrm{SMs}|\cdot T_{\mathrm{par}}},\qquad\epsilon_{p}^{\text{SNACK-COO}}>\epsilon_{p}^{\text{standard}}

improves because TparSNACK-COO<TparstandardT_{\mathrm{par}}^{\text{SNACK-COO}}<T_{\mathrm{par}}^{\text{standard}} at small nn. Atomic adds are required when multiple non-zeros write to the same output row, but the batch-wise block organization confines contention to one output column per block, reducing it relative to the row-wise scheme. Threads within a block process consecutive non-zeros for the same column bb, which also improves cache locality on BB.

Uniform Initializer cost (Algorithm 2).

Algorithm 2 draws n​n​z=(1−η)​m​knnz=(1-\eta)\,mk unique pairs by rejection: at step ii, the probability of drawing a fresh pair is pi=1−i/(m​k)p_{i}=1-i/(mk), giving a geometric expected number of trials of 𝔼⁡[1/pi]=m​k/(m​k−i)\mathbb{E}[1/p_{i}]=mk/(mk-i). Summing over the n​n​znnz steps,

𝔼⁡[trials]=∑i=0(1−η)​m​km​km​k−i≈∫0(1−η)​m​km​km​k−i​𝑑i=−m​k​ln⁡η,η∈(0,1),\mathbb{E}[\text{trials}]=\sum_{i=0}^{(1-\eta)mk}\frac{mk}{mk-i}\;\approx\;\int_{0}^{(1-\eta)mk}\frac{mk}{mk-i}\,di=-mk\ln\eta,\qquad\eta\in(0,1),

where the harmonic approximation ∑i=ab1/i≈ln⁡(b/a)\sum_{i=a}^{b}1/i\approx\ln(b/a) is used. The initializer is therefore essentially linear in n​n​znnz, and the rejection penalty ζ=𝔼[trials]/nnz=−lnη/(1−η)\zeta=\mathbb{E}[\text{trials}]/nnz=-\ln\eta/(1-\eta) is bounded: ζ→1\zeta\to 1 as η→1\eta\to 1 (very sparse, almost no collisions), and ζ\zeta grows only logarithmically as η\eta shrinks toward the dense regime.

Full gradient derivation (Section 3.4).

For a SNACK layer with sparse W∈ℝm×nW\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}, input X∈ℝn×bX\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times b}, and pre-activation A=W​X∈ℝm×bA=WX\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times b}, the chain rule gives

∂ℒ∂W=∂ℒ∂A∂A∂W=∇A⋅X⊤,∂ℒ∂X=(∂A∂X)⊤∂ℒ∂A=W⊤∇A,\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial W}=\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial A}\,\frac{\partial A}{\partial W}=\nabla A\cdot X^{\top},\qquad\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial X}=\Bigl(\frac{\partial A}{\partial X}\Bigr)^{\!\!\top}\!\!\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial A}=W^{\top}\,\nabla A,

where ∇A=∂ℒ/∂A∈ℝm×b\nabla A=\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times b}. The input-gradient term W⊤∇AW^{\top}\nabla A is sparse-times-dense and reuses SNACK-COO directly: W⊤W^{\top} inherits WW’s sparsity by swapping row and column index arrays, introducing no new non-zeros. Expanding the weight-gradient product entry-wise,

(∂ℒ∂W)i,j=∑t=1b∇Ai,tXj,t,\Bigl(\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial W}\Bigr)_{i,j}=\sum_{t=1}^{b}\nabla A_{i,t}\,X_{j,t},

which is a sum of bb rank-1 outer products: ∂ℒ/∂W=∑t=1b∇A(t)(X(t))⊤\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial W=\sum_{t=1}^{b}\nabla A^{(t)}(X^{(t)})^{\top}. A dense backward evaluates all m​nmn entries of this matrix; SNACK evaluates only (i,j)∈supp⁡(W)(i,j)\in\mathrm{supp}(W), since entries outside the support are zeroed by the sparsity mask and contribute nothing to the SGD update. This drops the per-step cost from 𝒪⁡(m​n​b)\mathcal{O}(mnb) to 𝒪⁡(n​n​z⋅b)\mathcal{O}(nnz\cdot b). Activation functions act element-wise on AA and are unaffected by WW’s sparsity [17].

Implementation plumbing (Section 3.5).

The SNACK-COO kernel parallelizes over sparse-matrix cells rather than over batch entries, which saturates the SMs from the non-zero workload alone and is what makes the kernel favorable at small nn. Within a block we issue __syncthreads() before atomic writes to avoid races, and we use T=256T=256 threads per block as a default that balances occupancy against scheduling overhead. The CUDA launch is wrapped in a C++/Torch extension that converts the COO triple from PyTorch tensors to flat float/int arrays and back. The sparse outer-product gradient is a separate one-dimensional CUDA kernel that loops over the n​n​znnz entries of supp⁡(W)\mathrm{supp}(W) and writes back the accumulated ∑t∇Ai,tXj,t\sum_{t}\nabla A_{i,t}X_{j,t} for each entry. The PyTorch nn.Module wraps both kernels behind a custom torch.autograd.Function, accepts a pluggable Initializer (default: the C++ uniform initializer of Algorithm 2), and stores weights as the COO triple (𝐀v,𝐀r,𝐀c)(\mathbf{A}_{v},\mathbf{A}_{r},\mathbf{A}_{c}) on-device for the entire training run.

End-to-end sparsity.

Across the full pipeline, SNACK preserves true sparsity at every step: (i) the forward pass runs SpMM (SNACK-COO by default, or any pluggable backend) directly on the COO triple and never expands WW to dense; (ii) the backward pass uses the sparse outer product over supp⁡(W)\mathrm{supp}(W) and never instantiates the m×nm\times n weight-gradient matrix; (iii) DST topology updates use the uniform initializer of Algorithm 2, which draws non-zeros directly with no dense m×km\times k probability tensor. Consequently no step of training or inference allocates a dense m×nm\times n weight or gradient tensor, which is the property the memory and energy measurements of Sections 4–5 exploit.

Appendix G GAMLP Graph-Workload Training Setup

This appendix details the training recipe behind the GAMLP-shaped sparse-inference results of Table 6 (Section 5). Inference is reported at batch =1=1 on the trained sparse weights; training itself is run at the natural mini-batch size for graph workloads, b=4096b=4096, where the leading dimension is no longer “small” relative to the layer width and SNACK-COO’s batch-to-SM mapping ceases to be the right fit. We therefore train through the SNACK layer with a Sputnik SpMM backend, which dominates at moderate sparsity and large batches [14], and only swap to SNACK-COO at inference time. This is exactly the backend-agnostic story of Section 3: the SNACK layer is fixed (sparse outer-product gradient, uniform initializer, COO weights), and the SpMM backend is chosen per regime.

Model and data.

We use R_GAMLP_RLU [57] on the OGB ogbn-products node-classification benchmark [20], with hidden dimension 512512, 55 feature-propagation hops, and 2/2/22/2/2 layers in the three GAMLP stages (default R_GAMLP_RLU configuration). Pre-processing, residual connections, and batch norm are enabled; dropout, attention dropout, and label dropout are 0.50.5, with α=0.5\alpha=0.5 for the residual mix. The sparsifiable substrate is the 5000×50005000{\times}5000 feature-head projection used at inference; embeddings, label propagation, and the classification head are kept dense.

Optimization.

Training uses the Adam optimizer at learning rate 10−310^{-3} with cross-entropy loss for 4040 epochs at batch size 40964096 on a single GPU. We use the same dense GAMLP hyperparameters as the public reference and only swap the feature-head projection from a dense nn.Linear to a SNACK module with the Sputnik backend; everything else (input pipeline, scheduler, weight decay, seed) follows the upstream GAMLP defaults. Dense and Dense+Mask baselines for the same backbone are trained under an identical recipe, the only difference being the feature-head implementation.

Sparsity schedule and DST.

Each run is initialized at its target sparsity η∈{0.9,0.95,0.99}\eta\in\{0.9,0.95,0.99\} and trained with a magnitude-based prune-and-grow update: every 55 epochs (until epoch 2525), we prune the ζ=5%\zeta=5\% smallest-magnitude non-zeros and regrow an equal number of unique (i,j)(i,j) coordinates with the uniform connection initializer of Algorithm 2. After epoch 2525 the topology is frozen and only weight values continue to update, which gives the optimizer a stable support to converge on. The inference results in Table 6 use the resulting frozen SNACK checkpoints, loaded directly into the SNACK-COO inference path with no re-pruning.

Why Sputnik for training and SNACK-COO for inference.

SNACK-COO’s parallel-efficiency analysis (Appendix F) shows the kernel’s advantage relies on n≪mn\ll m, i.e. batch much smaller than the layer width. At training-time batch 40964096 that condition is reversed and Sputnik’s structured-sparse SpMM is the better fit; at inference-time batch 11 the condition is restored and SNACK-COO is the better fit. Both paths use the same SNACK layer, the same COO weights, and the same outer-product gradient; only the SpMM backend changes. This is the concrete realization of the backend-agnostic claim made in Section 3.5 and explains why the same module can deliver Table 4’s training memory savings under Sputnik and Table 6’s inference speedups under SNACK-COO. The full training script and reproducibility commands are available at https://github.com/JafarBadour/Snack-SNN under experiments/gamlp_snack_benchmark/.

Empirical validation of the per-regime backend choice (Table 13).

The GAMLP training measurements directly back the argument above: at the natural graph-training batch 40964096, the layer-width-to-batch ratio violates SNACK-COO’s n≪mn\ll m assumption, and SNACK-COO accordingly pays a ≈9.4×\approx 9.4\times per-step latency tax (160.39160.39 vs. 17.1117.11 ms) and a ≈10×\approx 10\times per-step energy tax (17,17717{,}177 vs. 1,7001{,}700 mJ) over Dense. This is precisely the regime the paragraph above flags as Sputnik’s territory, which is why the recommended per-regime configuration trains the SNACK layer through the Sputnik backend at b=4096b=4096 (whose moderate-sparsity, large-batch dominance is documented in [14] and reproduced in our A100 sweeps in Appendix D.2, where the Sputnik variants overtake SNACK-COO from 5000×50005000{\times}5000 upward at batch 44) and only swaps to the SNACK-COO backend at the inference-time batch 11 regime, which is the configuration whose memory and latency we report in Table 6. Peak training memory is already minimally smaller for SNACK-COO (67846784 vs. 68236823 MB for Dense); the modest gap is consistent with the architectural ceiling noted in Section 5: only the 5000×50005000{\times}5000 feature-head projection is sparsified while the rest of the GAMLP backbone (multi-hop feature propagation buffers, embeddings, classifier head) remains dense. Validation accuracy is essentially matched: SNACK-COO reaches 0.91010.9101 final / 0.91720.9172 best vs. Dense+Mask’s 0.91400.9140 final / 0.91740.9174 best, a sub-half-point gap that is independent of the SpMM backend, since both SNACK-COO and SNACK(Sputnik) share the same uniform sparse initializer, sparse outer-product gradient, and magnitude prune-and-grow schedule, so any kernel-level swap is mathematically a reordering and will not move accuracy materially. The remaining accuracy headroom is a DST-recipe question (initialization, prune-and-grow schedule, dropout/regularization), orthogonal to the kernel contribution of this paper.
